explanations.explanation: I get why you'd go there, because seven was Peter's own number. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, asked, "Up to seven times?" But Jesus doesn't say "yep, seven's plenty." He answers, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!” (Matthew 18:22). Peter showed up with his number, and Jesus handed him a much bigger one.

Right, seven is not where Jesus lands. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, asked if seven times was the limit. Jesus told him, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!” (Matthew 18:22). I think Peter was hoping for a high five, and he walked away with homework instead.

That's the number in the text: “…a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him.” (Matthew 18:24). Say it slowly, friend, because it's a mountain of a number. I think that debt is meant to feel enormous. That's a long way from pocket change.

Five is a lot smaller than what the text says. The servant owes ten thousand talents (Matthew 18:24). That's a whole different pile of money. If he'd only owed five, he might have had a fighting chance of paying it back.

You're close to a number that does show up in this story, but it belongs to someone else. A hundred is what the fellow servant owes later, and that debt is counted in denarii, not talents (Matthew 18:28). The first servant owes ten thousand talents (Matthew 18:24). Easy to cross those wires when two big numbers are flying around.

explanations.answer: Sell him and his family and everything
explanations.explanation: That's what the master orders: that the man “…be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned.” (Matthew 18:25). It's a hard moment, and I think this one hurts. The debt is so big that his whole household is on the line. Hold onto that, because it makes what happens next hit even harder.

explanations.answer: Make him work off the whole debt
explanations.explanation: A payment plan would have been nice, but that's not what the master orders. The text says he orders the man sold, “…along with his wife and children and everything he owned.” (Matthew 18:25). Nothing in the story offers him a work schedule. I think this is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Send him away from the kingdom
explanations.explanation: The master doesn't send him away, though that's a reasonable guess. What he orders is that the servant be sold to pay his debt, “…along with his wife and children and everything he owned.” (Matthew 18:25). The sentence is about money owed and a household at risk. It's a heavy moment, and the story just states it plainly.

explanations.answer: Falls on his knees and begs
explanations.explanation: Down he goes. “Then the servant fell on his knees before him. ‘Have patience with me,’ he begged, ‘and I will pay back everything.’” (Matthew 18:26). He doesn't argue or sneak off, he just asks. Remember how that begging sounds, because it comes back around later.

No running here. The text puts him right in front of the master, on his knees (Matthew 18:26). He begs, “Have patience with me…” and promises to pay back everything. I've never been good at running anyway, since I come with a gold base attached.

The text never has him point a finger at anybody. He falls on his knees before the master and begs, “Have patience with me…” (Matthew 18:26). It's just him and his request. No other servants get dragged into it, at least not yet.

Yes, all of it. “His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him.” (Matthew 18:27). The servant had asked for patience and promised to pay it all back. What he got was the whole debt wiped out. I'd have needed a minute to sit down after that.

This one is true, friend, and it's a big moment. The text says, “His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him.” (Matthew 18:27). The servant only asked for more time. The master forgave the whole debt and let him go.

That would be the happy ending, but the story goes the other way. When the servant went out, he found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii. “He grabbed him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe me!’” (Matthew 18:28). He had just been forgiven so much, and he still didn't cancel this debt.

He does not cancel it. When that servant went out, he grabbed his fellow servant, began to choke him and said, “Pay back what you owe me!” (Matthew 18:28). He had just been forgiven so much. I'd call that a rough turn in the story.

Prison is the word. The forgiven servant “…went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.” (Matthew 18:30). The fellow servant had begged for patience and promised to pay. It wasn't enough for this man.

Slavery isn't what happens to the fellow servant. The master ordered the first servant sold, along with his wife and children and everything he owned (Matthew 18:25). The text says the forgiven servant “…went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.” (Matthew 18:30). It's easy to mix up the two debts, since there are two servants and two begging scenes.

Exile isn't in this story at all. The forgiven servant refused and “…went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.” (Matthew 18:30). So the fellow servant is locked up, not sent away. Next time, I'd go with the word the text actually uses.

They go straight to the master. The text says the fellow servants “…were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master.” (Matthew 18:31). They saw what happened, and they didn't keep it to themselves. Whatever happens next, the master is going to hear all of it.

Nice thought, but the text doesn't send them home. They “…were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master.” (Matthew 18:31). The master is the one who hears it. The families don't come into the story at this point.

Neighbors don't show up anywhere in this story. These servants were “greatly distressed” and “…went and recounted all of this to their master.” (Matthew 18:31). They took it straight to him. A group chat would've been faster, but the text says they went to their master.

explanations.answer: Shown him mercy the way he was shown mercy
explanations.explanation: That's the question the master asks: “Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?” (Matthew 18:33). It's the same mercy the servant had just been given. The master isn't asking for anything fancy. He's asking him to pass on what he got.

explanations.answer: Brought the matter to the master first
explanations.explanation: The master never says that. His question is, “Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?” (Matthew 18:33). The servant could have shown mercy right there, as soon as his fellow servant begged. No paperwork required.

explanations.answer: Let the other servants settle the debt
explanations.explanation: The master doesn't bring the other servants into it that way. The other servants only report what happened (Matthew 18:31). What the master asks is, “Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?” (Matthew 18:33). It all comes down to mercy given the way mercy was received.

Heart is the word Jesus uses: “…unless you forgive your brother from your heart.” (Matthew 18:35). He's pointing at something deeper than the words you say. This is the end of the story, and it's the point He wants Peter and us to carry out of the kitchen. And it answers Peter's question from the start. Forgiveness isn't a number to count.

Close, since lips are where the words come out. But Jesus says “…from your heart.” (Matthew 18:35). Saying it is one thing, and He is talking about something deeper. I've said "I'm fine" through a mouthful of cookie plenty of times, so I know the difference.

The head is a fair guess, since forgiving can feel like a decision you make. But Jesus says, “…unless you forgive your brother from your heart.” (Matthew 18:35). So it's more than knowing you should forgive. It's from the heart, friend.
